title: EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report highlights, week ending 2026-09-25
text:
[Transcribed from https://ir.eia.gov/wpsr/summary.txt as retrieved 2026-10-03 (release of 2026-09-30).]
For the week ending September 25, 2026, U.S. refineries processed 16.3 million barrels per day (b/d), down 554,000 b/d from the previous week, at 92.5% capacity utilization. Gasoline output averaged 9.5 million b/d, and distillate production decreased to 5.0 million b/d. 

Crude oil imports decreased 179,000 b/d to 5.7 million b/d, although the four-week average of 6.4 million b/d is 4.8% above the year-ago level. Gasoline imports averaged 500,000 b/d; distillate imports averaged 153,000 b/d. 

Commercial crude oil inventories (excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve) increased 0.9 million barrels to 427.3 million barrels, 2% above the five-year average. Gasoline inventories decreased 1.7 million barrels, 7% below the five-year average. Distillate inventories decreased 2.3 million barrels, 14% below the five-year average. Propane/propylene inventories increased 1.8 million barrels, 20% above the five-year average. Total commercial petroleum inventories decreased by 7.0 million barrels for the week.

Over the past four weeks, total product supplied averaged 20.8 million b/d, up 2.1% year over year. The four-week average for gasoline product supplied increased 0.3% year over year to 8.7 million b/d, while the four-week average for distillate product supplied increased 5.2% to 3.8 million b/d. The four-week average for jet fuel product supplied increased 6.5% year over year.

title: Our 2010–2024 study of inventories and WTI curve structure
text:
Weekly sample 2010-01-08 – 2024-03-29 (743 WPSR weeks). Prices taken at the Wednesday WPSR release date (prior trading day if a holiday). Inventory variables are **actual** weekly changes; without consensus forecasts these are not surprises, and the results are associations, not causal estimates.
1. **Stock levels explain curve structure; weekly changes barely do.** Deviations of Cushing and total US crude stocks from seasonal norms explain 36% of the variation in WTI M1–M2, with Cushing the stronger variable: each 1 mb of Cushing below normal goes with ~$0.029/bbl more backwardation, and the tightest Cushing quartile was backwardated 82% of the time vs 1% in the loosest.
2. **Weekly inventory changes have the expected sign but little explanatory power** (R² 0.03 for the spread, 0.03 for returns). A 1 mb Cushing draw goes with ~$0.031/bbl spread tightening; headline crude changes are not significant for the spread. Without consensus data, these are actual changes, not surprises.
3. **No significant evidence that Cushing changes matter more when Cushing is tight** (interaction p = 0.19). The point estimate has the expected sign, but the data do not support claiming a regime difference.
4. **Brent–WTI is wider when Cushing is tight and US exports are high** (2016+), consistent with WTI pricing as the export barrel that has to move overseas; this is an association.
